questions.prompt: Explain how identity, token scope and project membership combine into a write permission, and what happens when a token is revoked mid-session.

keyPoints.text: Authentication hashes the bearer string and finds an unrevoked token with that hash.
keyPoints.quote: hashes the bearer string and finds an unrevoked token with that hash

keyPoints.text: Scope limits the kind of operation; membership decides where the user may perform it.
keyPoints.quote: A token **scope** limits the *kind* of operation.

keyPoints.text: A write token held by a member of one project still cannot edit another project's flags.
The effective permission is the intersection of scope, role and membership.
keyPoints.quote: The effective permission is the intersection of scope, role and membership.

keyPoints.text: The wrapper picks the scope each call needs from the method name: create/update/delete/revoke/change methods need write, a fixed list of global operations needs admin, everything else read.
The browser explains permissions, but the server enforces them independently.
The write check is requireProjectWrite in the services module.

questions.prompt: Explain how a global revision plus a digest protects edits, why commit order matters for durability, and the trade-off of global revisioning.

keyPoints.text: The workspace has one global revision that editors send back with If-Match.
keyPoints.quote: The workspace has one global revision, `meta.version`.

keyPoints.text: Permission checks run against the request's frozen snapshot, so a concurrent commit makes the whole operation refused.
keyPoints.quote: the version or digest no longer matches and the whole operation is refused

keyPoints.text: Two editors changing unrelated records still conflict under a global revision.
keyPoints.quote: two editors changing unrelated records still conflict

keyPoints.text: A conflict differs from an uncertain response, where the server may already have accepted the request.
keyPoints.quote: A conflict is different from an uncertain response.

keyPoints.text: #commit writes to disk first and publishes to memory second: renameSync at line 249, then #accept at line 252.
keyPoints.quote: publishes the new state in memory only after `renameSync` has succeeded

keyPoints.text: The writer lease is a lock file opened with wx; a second writer gets EEXIST, which becomes 503.
keyPoints.quote: A second writer gets `EEXIST`, which becomes 503.

keyPoints.text: The comparison happens under the lease in the storage module.

questions.prompt: Explain why a snapshot ETag cannot stand in for an evaluation result, and how bucketing and missing context are handled.

keyPoints.text: The snapshot cache key names the configuration that was used, not who asked.
keyPoints.quote: It names the configuration that was used. It says nothing about which user asked.

keyPoints.text: One ETag maps to several different answers across contexts.
keyPoints.quote: One ETag maps to four different answers.

keyPoints.text: A 304 keyed on the ETag would hand one user another user's decision.
keyPoints.quote: would therefore give user A user D's decision

keyPoints.text: Bucketing is deterministic: the same user always lands in the same bucket and nothing is stored.
keyPoints.quote: The same user always lands in the same bucket, and nothing is stored.

keyPoints.text: Variant selection uses a different hash input so rollout position does not bias the variant.
keyPoints.quote: Being inside the rollout therefore does not bias which variant you get.

keyPoints.text: Missing or non-scalar context never matches, even through negation.
keyPoints.quote: Missing data cannot switch a flag on.
